questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At π/4 = 45° that point is (√2/2, √2/2), so cos(π/4) = √2/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(π/4) = √2/2.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(π/3)?
questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At π/3 = 60° that point is (1/2, √3/2), so cos(π/3) = 1/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(π/3) = √3/2.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(2π/3)?
questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At 2π/3 = 120° that point is (−1/2, √3/2), so cos(2π/3) = −1/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(2π/3) = √3/2.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(3π/4)?
questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At 3π/4 = 135° that point is (−√2/2, √2/2), so cos(3π/4) = −√2/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(3π/4) = √2/2.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(5π/6)?
questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At 5π/6 = 150° that point is (−√3/2, 1/2), so cos(5π/6) = −√3/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(5π/6) = 1/2.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(7π/6)?
questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At 7π/6 = 210° that point is (−√3/2, −1/2), so cos(7π/6) = −√3/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(7π/6) = −1/2.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(4π/3)?
questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At 4π/3 = 240° that point is (−1/2, −√3/2), so cos(4π/3) = −1/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(4π/3) = −√3/2.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(5π/3)?
questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At 5π/3 = 300° that point is (1/2, −√3/2), so cos(5π/3) = 1/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(5π/3) = −√3/2.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of cos(11π/6)?
questions.explanation: Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. At 11π/6 = 330° that point is (√3/2, −1/2), so cos(11π/6) = √3/2. Reading off the y-coordinate instead gives sin(11π/6) = −1/2.

questions.stem: In the first quadrant, which of sin θ, cos θ and tan θ are positive?
questions.explanation: In the first quadrant both coordinates are positive. Since cos θ is the x-coordinate, sin θ the y-coordinate and tan θ their quotient, that leaves all three positive.

questions.stem: In the second quadrant, which of sin θ, cos θ and tan θ are positive?
questions.explanation: In the second quadrant y is positive but x is negative. Since cos θ is the x-coordinate, sin θ the y-coordinate and tan θ their quotient, that leaves sin θ only positive.

questions.stem: In the third quadrant, which of sin θ, cos θ and tan θ are positive?
questions.explanation: In the third quadrant both coordinates are negative, so their quotient is positive. Since cos θ is the x-coordinate, sin θ the y-coordinate and tan θ their quotient, that leaves tan θ only positive.

questions.stem: In the fourth quadrant, which of sin θ, cos θ and tan θ are positive?
questions.explanation: In the fourth quadrant x is positive but y is negative. Since cos θ is the x-coordinate, sin θ the y-coordinate and tan θ their quotient, that leaves cos θ only positive.

questions.stem: To convert an angle from degrees to radians, you multiply by:
questions.explanation: A full turn is 360° and also 2π radians, so 180° = π radians and one degree is π/180 radians. Multiplying by 180/π goes the other way, turning radians into degrees — a good check is that the number should get smaller when converting degrees to radians.

questions.stem: To convert an angle from radians to degrees, you multiply by:
questions.explanation: Since π radians = 180°, one radian is 180/π degrees, which is a little under 60°. Multiplying by π/180 is the opposite conversion and would turn an already-small radian measure into a smaller one still.

questions.stem: A point on the unit circle has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ). What is the radius of that circle?
questions.explanation: The unit circle is defined as the circle of radius 1 centred at the origin — that is what "unit" means here. It is what makes the coordinates equal to cos θ and sin θ exactly, with no scaling factor: on a circle of radius r the point would be (r cos θ, r sin θ).

questions.stem: An angle of θ satisfies 0° < θ < 90°. Which quadrant is it in?
questions.explanation: Quadrants are counted anticlockwise from the positive x-axis in 90° steps, so 0° to 90° is the first quadrant. Counting clockwise instead is the usual mistake and reverses quadrants two and four.

questions.stem: An angle of θ satisfies 90° < θ < 180°. Which quadrant is it in?
questions.explanation: Quadrants are counted anticlockwise from the positive x-axis in 90° steps, so 90° to 180° is the second quadrant. Counting clockwise instead is the usual mistake and reverses quadrants two and four.

questions.stem: An angle of θ satisfies 180° < θ < 270°. Which quadrant is it in?
questions.explanation: Quadrants are counted anticlockwise from the positive x-axis in 90° steps, so 180° to 270° is the third quadrant. Counting clockwise instead is the usual mistake and reverses quadrants two and four.

questions.stem: An angle of θ satisfies 270° < θ < 360°. Which quadrant is it in?
questions.explanation: Quadrants are counted anticlockwise from the positive x-axis in 90° steps, so 270° to 360° is the fourth quadrant. Counting clockwise instead is the usual mistake and reverses quadrants two and four.

questions.stem: How many radians are there in one full turn?
questions.explanation: A full turn is 360°, and since 180° = π radians, a full turn is 2π radians. Answering π is the commonest slip — that is a half turn, which is why 180° and π are the pair worth memorising.

questions.stem: π radians is equal to how many degrees?
questions.explanation: π radians is a half turn, which is 180°. This single fact drives every other conversion: halve it for π/2 = 90°, double it for 2π = 360°.

questions.stem: What are the coordinates of the point at θ = 0 on the unit circle?
questions.explanation: At θ = 0 the point sits on the positive x-axis, one unit from the origin, so it is (1, 0). Since a point on the unit circle is (cos θ, sin θ), this says cos 0 = 1 and sin 0 = 0.

questions.stem: On the unit circle, the y-coordinate of a point gives you:
questions.explanation: A point on the unit circle is (cos θ, sin θ), so the x-coordinate is the cosine and the y-coordinate is the sine. Swapping the two is the single most common error in this topic; tan θ is their quotient, sin θ ÷ cos θ.

questions.stem: Which quadrant does an angle of θ = π/4 lie in?
questions.explanation: π/4 is 45°, which is between 0° and 90°, so it lies in the first quadrant. Both coordinates are positive there, and at 45° they are equal: (√2/2, √2/2).
